sources.title: Human History Map research coverage ledger
sources.note: One exact observed interval, one border file, no current summary or card, and unreviewed identity, chronology and border fields before this packet.

sources.title: Human History Map 2000 BCE borders
sources.note: Decoded exact nine-position polygon, bounds, component hash, sampled point ownership and neighbors for the only target interval.

sources.title: Human History Map 1500 BCE borders
sources.note: Confirms exact-id disappearance and redistribution among several unrelated editorial labels at the indexed endpoint.

sources.title: The Archaeology of the Tibetan Plateau
sources.note: Current archaeological synthesis emphasizes regional sequences and dedicates a chapter to transformations beginning around 2000 BCE rather than one plateau-wide culture.

sources.title: History of Research
sources.note: History of survey, excavation and interpretation on the plateau, useful for explaining uneven evidence and changing archaeological knowledge.

sources.title: The Archaeology of the Tibetan Plateau: contents and chapter chronology
sources.note: Publisher contents place early millet agriculture and eastern plateau occupation before about 1700 BCE in a distinct regional chapter.

sources.title: The new chronology and material culture of a second millennium BC Neolithic site in the heartland of the Tibetan Plateau: Qugong re-excavated
sources.note: Sichuan University account of seven new radiocarbon dates and Bayesian modeling that shifts the relevant Qugong deposits to roughly 1400 to 1300 BCE.

sources.title: Early agropastoral settlement and cultural change in central Tibet in the first millennium BC: excavations at Bangga
sources.note: Excavation report includes a cautious comparison of Qugong, Changguogou and later Bangga and exposes chronological limits on older site claims.

sources.title: Agriculture facilitated permanent human occupation of the Tibetan Plateau after 3600 B.P.
sources.note: Radiocarbon-dated crops and settlement distributions connect cold-tolerant barley, wheat and livestock with sustained higher-elevation occupation after about 1600 BCE.

sources.title: Early evidence for the use of wheat and barley as staple crops on the margins of the Tibetan Plateau
sources.note: Direct crop dates and archaeobotanical evidence trace changing millet, wheat and barley use while identifying major gaps around 2000 to 1700 BCE.

sources.title: Moving agriculture onto the Tibetan plateau: the archaeobotanical evidence
sources.note: Peking University repository record for a synthesis of Karuo millet, later barley-wheat systems, caprines and complementary wild foods.

sources.title: A Study on Ancient Barley, Wheat and Millet Discovered at Changguo of Tibet
sources.note: Published crop identification at Changguogou; important regional context whose location and chronology must not be stretched across the map.

sources.title: Barley heads east: Genetic analyses reveal routes of spread through diverse Eurasian landscapes
sources.note: Plant genetics and direct dates show several possible barley dispersal routes and the oldest dated Chinese barley around 2000 BCE in northeastern Qinghai.

sources.title: Journey to the east: Diverse routes and variable flowering times for wheat and barley en route to prehistoric China
sources.note: Combines crop genetics and archaeobotanical dates while explicitly noting missing third-millennium evidence across southern Tibet.

sources.title: Geospatial modelling of farmer to herder interactions maps cultural geography of Bronze and Iron Age Tibet, 3600 to 2200 BP
sources.note: Archaeological distribution modeling finds multiple interaction zones and ecological strategies, never one civilization border.

sources.title: Radiocarbon chronology and settlement patterns in the Bronze Age of the Qaidam Basin, Northwestern China
sources.note: Survey, dating, charred crops, grinding tools and fauna support flexible agropastoral lifeways in a northern basin, mostly later than this interval.

sources.title: Paleoproteomic evidence reveals dairying supported prehistoric occupation of the highland Tibetan Plateau
sources.note: Dental-calculus proteomics, dates and Gepaseru burial context distinguish possible milking around 1883 to 1691 BCE from direct goat-milk peptides after 1500 BCE.

sources.title: Research reveals the history of dairy consumption among ancient Tibetan Plateau populations
sources.note: Sichuan University explanation of dental-calculus paleoproteomics and the population range of later direct dairy evidence.

sources.title: The Genome Landscape of Tibetan Sheep Reveals Adaptive Introgression from Argali and the History of Early Human Settlements
sources.note: Livestock-genome research paired with archaeological distributions, useful only when animal lineage is kept separate from human language and ethnicity.

sources.title: Zooarchaeology, ancient mtDNA, and radiocarbon dating provide new evidence for domestic cattle and caprines in the Tao River Valley
sources.note: Directly dates sheep around 1900 to 1750 BCE and goats around 1600 to 1450 BCE in Gansu-Qinghai, outside much of the polygon but relevant to regional exchange.

sources.title: Lake-centred sedentary lifestyle of early Tibetan Plateau Indigenous populations at high elevation 4,400 years ago
sources.note: Excavation, isotopes and ancient DNA document fishing, hunting, bone tools and small-scale crop exchange at Mabu Co around 2450 to 2050 BCE, just before the atlas interval.

sources.title: Ancient genomes from the Himalayas illuminate the genetic history of Tibetans and their Tibeto-Burman speaking neighbors
sources.note: Ancient Himalayan genomes beginning around 1494 BCE reveal population history while warning against treating present language categories as ancient genetic labels.

sources.title: Human genetic history on the Tibetan Plateau in the past 5100 years
sources.note: Eighty-nine ancient genomes show shared plateau ancestry, strong regional structure and interaction; genes cannot identify a prehistoric language or map border.

sources.title: Ancient genomes reveal basal Asian ancestries and dynamic population interactions over time on the southern Tibetan Plateau
sources.note: Sixteen Mabu Co genomes and regional comparisons reveal continuity plus interaction without naming a single ethnic population.

sources.title: Ancient mitogenomes show plateau populations from last 5200 years partially contributed to present-day Tibetans
sources.note: Ancient mitochondrial sequences support partial, not complete, ancestry continuity and demonstrate why modern identities cannot simply be projected backward.

sources.title: Altitude adaptation in Tibetans caused by introgression of Denisovan-like DNA
sources.note: Identifies Denisovan-related EPAS1 ancestry involved in modern high-altitude physiology, deep biological history that cannot label Bronze Age artifacts.

sources.title: Denisovans and Homo sapiens on the Tibetan Plateau: dispersals and adaptations
sources.note: Review separates very ancient hominin occupation, later human settlement, physiology and cultural adaptations.

sources.title: The earliest human occupation of the high-altitude Tibetan Plateau 40 thousand to 30 thousand years ago
sources.note: Excavated stone artifacts at Nwya Devu demonstrate very deep use of the high plateau within the polygon, tens of millennia before this card.

sources.title: Permanent human occupation of the central Tibetan Plateau in the early Holocene
sources.note: Dating of Chusang hand- and footprints illustrates early plateau presence and the importance of contested chronometric methods.

sources.title: Middle and Late Pleistocene Denisovan subsistence at Baishiya Karst Cave
sources.note: Zooarchaeology and proteomics reveal very ancient animal use on the plateau and provide methodological background, not an ancestry label for 2000 BCE.

sources.title: Direct dating of lithic surface artifacts using luminescence
sources.note: Explains optically stimulated luminescence dating of buried stone artifacts and its geomorphic controls.

sources.title: Foraging and farming: archaeobotanical and zooarchaeological evidence for Neolithic exchange on the Tibetan Plateau
sources.note: Plants, animals, ceramics and graves at Zongri reveal interaction between foragers and farmers near the northeastern plateau margin.

sources.title: Karuo archaeological site
sources.note: Chinese encyclopedia record dates the Qamdo-area settlement about 3300 to 2100 BCE and lists its excavation and protected-site status.

sources.title: Dating Human Settlement in the East-Central Tibetan Plateau during the Late Holocene
sources.note: Radiocarbon audit finds only one genuinely Bronze Age human among twelve surveyed Yushu sites, demonstrating severe chronology and sampling limits.

sources.title: On the early metal objects and early Metal Age in Tibet
sources.note: Review treats early copper, bronze, iron and composite objects as a complicated technological history rather than a migration label.

sources.title: Reassessing early metallurgy in northwest China
sources.note: University of Science and Technology Beijing review separates metallurgical stages around 2300 to 1500 BCE and regional variation within Qijia contexts.

sources.title: New Evidence for Prehistoric Textile Production and Social Complexity on the Southeastern Tibetan Plateau
sources.note: Spindle whorls, loom evidence and fabric traces document skilled textile production while leaving worker gender open.

sources.title: Bioarchaeological profile of stress and dental disease among ancient high altitude Himalayan communities of Nepal
sources.note: Teeth and skeletons demonstrate how stress and dental disease can be studied while remaining site- and period-specific.

sources.title: Sding Chung: an early multi-burial cave site on the Tibetan Plateau
sources.note: A later multi-burial cave demonstrates regional mortuary diversity and the limits of inferring belief or kinship directly from graves.

sources.title: Fuel-use strategies at ultrahigh elevations on the Tibetan Plateau since the last deglaciation
sources.note: Charcoal and combustion evidence track changing fuel choices at plateau sites, with strict local and chronological limits.

sources.title: Grasslands of the World: The Tibetan Steppe
sources.note: Institutional ecological overview of cold desert, steppe, meadow, river headwaters and grazing constraints, used only as environmental comparison.

sources.title: Palaeoenvironmental proxies indicate long-term development of agro-pastoralist landscapes in Inner Asian mountains
sources.note: Pollen, charcoal and sediment proxies show long human-environment interaction rather than a single migration or abrupt economic replacement.

sources.title: The emergence, development, and impact of prehistoric agriculture on the Tibetan plateau
sources.note: Recent synthesis distinguishes successive millet, mixed and barley-wheat systems with strong spatial and chronological variation.

sources.title: Dated language phylogenies shed light on the ancestry of Sino-Tibetan
sources.note: One model dates family dispersal while explicitly describing disputed basal topology and much later dates of Tibetan and Burmese texts.

sources.title: Phylogenetic evidence for Sino-Tibetan origin in northern China in the Late Neolithic
sources.note: A different Bayesian lexical analysis favors a northern origin and a Sinitic versus Tibeto-Burman split, one debated model rather than a map of speakers.

sources.title: Dated phylogeny suggests early Neolithic origin of Sino-Tibetan languages
sources.note: Alternative clock analysis estimates a broad root-age interval and tests multiple subgroup structures, illustrating model uncertainty.

sources.title: Glottolog 5.3: Sino-Tibetan
sources.note: Current reference catalogue displays hundreds of languages and a branching classification, not one homogeneous Tibeto-Burman people.

sources.title: Tibeto-Burman classification
sources.note: Classic linguistic discussion stresses major internal diversity and unresolved subgrouping; its taxonomy is a scholarly model, not archaeological identity.

sources.title: Cave 17: the Library Cave; the Tibetan annals
sources.note: British Library International Dunhuang Programme places surviving Old Tibetan documentary culture in the imperial era, far after this interval.

proposedOverrides.summary: A cautious archaeological guide to diverse High Asian communities hidden beneath an anachronistic 2000 to 1500 BCE language-family label, with every site, date and inference kept local.
